lessons.title: അധ്യാപകന്റെ (adhyāpakanṟe) — "the teacher's"
lessons.gloss: the teacher's — the ending that was inside "my" all along, now put on any noun

needs: your eyes, because the lesson points at something written down
notice.text: Before we start: this one needs your eyes, so it is not fully a driving lesson. You will want your eyes, because the lesson points at something written down. You can listen to all of it now and come back to the parts that need looking at once you have stopped.

segments.text: Say my. Then say the word for teacher.
You have owned the first of those since the second chapter, and you have never been able to do to any other word what it does.

blocks.title: Grammar Lens: the ending was there all along

segments.text: എന്റെ was handed to you whole, as a single word meaning my. Look at its end:
-ന്റെ is a suffix, and it makes whatever it lands on the owner. That is the one thing this lesson adds, and it turns a word you memorised into a machine you can run.
അധ്യാപകന്റെ പുസ്തകം adhyāpakanṟe pustakaṁ — "the teacher's book".
The owner comes first, wearing the ending; the thing owned follows bare. English does the same with 's and the opposite with of. Malayalam only has the first order.
The script lesson for എന്റെ already showed you ന്റെ on its own, as a conjunct to read. It was a piece of writing then. It is a piece of grammar now, and it is the same piece.
That is worth expecting from this language: something introduced as a shape often turns out later to be a part.

segments.instruction: at എന്റെ and അധ്യാപകന്റെ (adhyāpakanṟe), and find where they agree
segments.source: [YOU LOOK: at **എന്റെ** and **അധ്യാപകന്റെ**, and find where they agree]

segments.instruction: which of the two words in the phrase is the owner
segments.source: [YOU SAY: which of the two words in the phrase is the owner]

segments.text: What does -ന്റെ do to a noun? (Makes it the owner.) How do you say the teacher's book? (അധ്യാപകന്റെ (adhyāpakanṟe) പുസ്തകം.) And which comes first, the owner or the thing? (The owner.)

lessons.title: അമ്മയുടെ (ammayuṭe) — "mother's"
lessons.gloss: mother's — the same job done by a different ending, chosen by the noun in front of it

segments.text: Say the teacher's book. Then take the ending off and say the teacher again on their own.

blocks.title: Grammar Lens: the same job, a different ending

segments.text: അമ്മയുടെ പുസ്തകം ammayuṭe pustakaṁ — "mother's book".
Not -ന്റെ. -ഉടെ, and a യ appears in front of it.
A noun that ends in a vowel takes -യുടെ. അമ്മ ends in a vowel, so that is the ending it gets. അധ്യാപകൻ ends in a consonant, so it took the other one.

utterances: noun ends in: a consonant. ending: -ന്റെ.
noun ends in: a vowel. ending: -യുടെ.

segments.text: You do not choose between them. The noun in front does, and it decides by its last sound rather than by anything you mean. So the question to ask is never which ending do I want — it is what does this word end in.

segments.instruction: both owners in a row — adhyāpakanṟe, ammayuṭe
segments.source: [YOU SAY: both owners in a row — *adhyāpakanṟe*, *ammayuṭe*]

segments.instruction: what decided which ending each one took
segments.source: [YOU SAY: what decided which ending each one took]

segments.text: Which ending does a vowel-final noun take? (-യുടെ.) How do you say mother's book? (അമ്മയുടെ (ammayuṭe) പുസ്തകം.) And who picks the ending — you, or the noun? (The noun.)

lessons.title: (whose it is) (ārute enna ōrmma) — from cold
lessons.gloss: cold retrieval of both genitive endings and of what decides between them

segments.text: Close the lessons before this one. Say my, and then say what its last piece does when you put it on somebody else.

blocks.title: Grammar Lens: two endings, one job, and the noun decides

utterances: owner: അധ്യാപകന്റെ (adhyāpakanṟe). ending: -ന്റെ. because it ends in: a consonant.
owner: അമ്മയുടെ (ammayuṭe). ending: -യുടെ. because it ends in: a vowel.

segments.text: One job — whose it is — and the choice is made by the last sound of the noun, not by you.
Then the phrase is built the same way every time: owner first with the ending, thing second and bare. adhyāpakanṟe pustakaṁ, ammayuṭe pustakaṁ.
A third possessor, and every one after it.

എന്റെ and നിന്റെ were handed over whole — my and your, two words to memorise. Naming the ending inside them turns a closed pair into an open rule: any noun this book has taught you can now own something.
That is the difference between a word and a piece of grammar, and it is worth looking for: when two words you were given separately end the same way, the ending is usually doing the work.

segments.instruction: which ending each took, and what decided it
segments.source: [YOU SAY: which ending each took, and what decided it]

segments.instruction: my book, using the word you have had since the second chapter
segments.source: [YOU SAY: *my book*, using the word you have had since the second chapter]

segments.instruction: which comes first in the phrase, the owner or the thing
segments.source: [YOU SAY: which comes first in the phrase, the owner or the thing]

segments.text: Which ending follows a consonant? (-ന്റെ.) Which follows a vowel? (-യുടെ.) And what does either one do to the noun it lands on? (Makes it the owner.)
